You are required to make a serial dilution of the 1% glucose solution, G, which reduces the
concentration by half between each successive dilution.
You will need to prepare 10 cm of each concentration.
Fig. 1.1 shows the first two beakers you will use to make your serial dilution.

Proceed as follows:
1. Set up a water-bath and heat to boiling ready for step 6.
2. Prepare the concentrations of glucose solution as shown in Fig. 1.1.
3. Put 2 cm of 1% glucose solution into a test-tube.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text:
State the smallest division on the syringe you used in step 3.
State the actual error when using this syringe.

Calculate the percentage error when using this syringe.
You may lose marks if you do not show your working.
percentage error ______
4. Put 2 cm of Benedict’s solution into the same test-tube as step 3.
5. Shake the test-tube gently to mix the contents.
Read step 6 to step 9 before proceeding.
You are required to:
• observe the contents of the test-tube continuously while the test-tube is heated for
60 seconds
• record the time taken for the first appearance of a colour change, if a colour change
occurs during this 60 seconds
• record the colour after heating for 60 seconds.
6. Put this test-tube into the water-bath you prepared in step 1 and start timing.
7. Record the time taken for the first appearance of a colour change in Table 1.1.
Do not stop the clock and continue heating until 60 seconds.
If there is no colour change after 60 seconds record the time as ‘more than 60’.
8. At 60 seconds remove the test-tube from the water-bath, gently shake, and record the colour
of the Benedict’s solution in Table 1.1.
9. Repeat step 3 to step 8 for each of the glucose solutions you prepared in step 2.
You are not required to repeat this experiment.

A scientist studied the change in the concentration of glucose in blood plasma after eating a
meal containing carbohydrate. Samples of blood plasma were taken at regular intervals after
eating the meal and the concentration of glucose in each sample was measured.
The results are shown in Table 1.2.

between 60 minutes and 80 minutes after eating the meal.

text: Glucose is an important substrate for cellular respiration. Glucose is absorbed into the blood from
the small intestine and transported in the blood plasma to the body cells.
• prepare different concentrations of the glucose solution G
• carry out the Benedict’s test on each of the concentrations of glucose solution you have
• carry out the Benedict’s test on the solution representing blood plasma P
• use the results of the Benedict’s tests to estimate the concentration of glucose in P.
